q: You set width and padding on a box but the total width is larger than expected. Why?
options: Padding is ignored by default in CSS
By default width only applies to content — padding is added on top
You need to set margin to 0 first
Width and padding cannot be used together
explain: The default box model adds padding on top of the declared width. Use box-sizing: border-box to include padding and border inside the declared width.

q: You want padding and border included in an element's width. What CSS property do you set?
options: box-model: border-box
box-sizing: border-box
width: include-padding
padding-box: true
explain: box-sizing: border-box makes the declared width include padding and border. This is now standard practice and most resets apply it to all elements.

q: What is the difference between margin and padding?
options: Margin is inside the element, padding is outside
Padding is space inside the element, margin is space outside
They are identical — just different names
Margin affects background color, padding does not
explain: Padding is the space between the content and the border. Margin is the space outside the border between the element and its neighbors.

q: You want to center a block element horizontally inside its parent. What is the classic way?
options: text-align: center on the element
margin: 0 auto on the element with a defined width
padding: auto on the parent
position: center on the element
explain: margin: 0 auto distributes available horizontal space equally on both sides. The element must have a defined width for this to work.

q: What does display: none do compared to visibility: hidden?
options: They are identical
display: none removes the element from layout, visibility: hidden hides it but keeps the space
visibility: hidden removes the element from layout, display: none keeps the space
display: none only works on block elements
explain: display: none removes the element entirely from the document flow. visibility: hidden makes it invisible but it still occupies space in the layout.

q: You apply a color to a parent element. The children inherit it without you setting it. Why?
options: All CSS properties are inherited by default
color is an inherited property — children use the parent value unless they set their own
You accidentally set color on the children too
Inheritance only works with class selectors
explain: Some CSS properties like color and font-size are inherited by default. Children use the parent's value unless they explicitly override it.

q: You want an element to sit next to another element on the same line. What display value do you use?
options: display: block
display: inline or display: inline-block
display: flex on the element itself
float: inline
explain: Block elements start on a new line. Inline and inline-block elements sit alongside other inline elements on the same line.

q: What is the difference between inline and inline-block?
options: inline-block allows setting width and height, inline does not
inline allows setting width and height, inline-block does not
They are identical
inline-block starts on a new line, inline does not
explain: Inline elements cannot have width or height set. Inline-block sits inline with other elements but respects width, height, padding and margin like a block element.

q: You set position: absolute on an element. What does it position relative to?
options: Always the viewport
The nearest ancestor with a position other than static
The body element always
The element's natural position in the flow
explain: Absolutely positioned elements are placed relative to their nearest positioned ancestor. If no ancestor has a position set they fall back to the initial containing block.

q: You want an element to stay visible in the same position as the user scrolls. What position value do you use?
options: position: absolute
position: static
position: fixed
position: sticky
explain: position: fixed anchors an element to the viewport so it stays in place during scrolling. position: sticky stays fixed only within its parent container.

q: What does z-index control?
options: The zoom level of an element
The stacking order of positioned elements along the z-axis
The horizontal position of an element
The number of layers in a CSS animation
explain: z-index controls which element appears in front when elements overlap. Higher values appear on top. It only works on elements with a position other than static.

q: You use em for font size. What is it relative to?
options: The root html element font size
The font size of the element's parent
The viewport width
The browser default font size always
explain: em is relative to the font size of the parent element. This means it compounds through nested elements. Use rem to always be relative to the root font size instead.

q: What does rem stand for and what is it relative to?
options: Relative em — relative to the parent element
Root em — relative to the font size of the html element
Responsive em — relative to the viewport
Reset em — resets to browser default
explain: rem stands for root em. It is always relative to the font size of the html element regardless of nesting. This makes it more predictable than em for sizing.

q: You want a CSS rule to apply only on screens narrower than 768px. What do you use?
options: screen-size: max(768px)
@media (max-width: 768px)
@responsive max-width: 768px
viewport: 768px
explain: Media queries let you apply CSS rules based on screen conditions. max-width: 768px targets screens up to 768px wide — typically mobile devices.

q: What is the specificity order from lowest to highest?
options: IDs, classes, elements, inline styles
Elements, classes, IDs, inline styles
Classes, elements, IDs, inline styles
Inline styles, IDs, classes, elements
explain: Specificity order from lowest to highest is element selectors, class selectors, ID selectors, then inline styles. Higher specificity wins when rules conflict.

q: You add a class and an ID selector for the same element with conflicting styles. Which wins?
options: The class selector — it is more commonly used
The ID selector — it has higher specificity
Whichever comes last in the stylesheet
They cancel each other out
explain: ID selectors have higher specificity than class selectors. The ID style wins regardless of source order. Use classes for reusable styles and avoid IDs for styling.

q: You set color: red on an element but another rule overrides it with color: blue. How do you force red to apply?
options: Add !important after the value
Move the rule to the bottom of the stylesheet
Use an ID selector instead of a class
Add priority: high to the rule
explain: !important overrides all other declarations regardless of specificity. Use it sparingly — it makes styles hard to debug and override later.

q: What is a CSS pseudo-class?
options: A fake class used for testing
A keyword added to a selector to style elements based on their state or position
A class that only applies on hover
A CSS variable that holds a class name
explain: Pseudo-classes like :hover, :focus, :first-child target elements based on state or position without adding extra HTML classes. They start with a single colon.

q: What is the difference between :hover and :focus?
options: They are identical
:hover triggers on mouse over, :focus triggers when an element receives keyboard or click focus
:focus only works on input elements
:hover works on mobile, :focus only works on desktop
explain: :hover applies when the mouse is over an element. :focus applies when an element is focused via keyboard tab or click. Both are important for accessibility.

q: You want to add a style to an element only when it is the first child of its parent. What pseudo-class do you use?
options: :first-element
:first-child
:first-of-type
:nth-child(0)
explain: :first-child selects an element only if it is the first child of its parent. :first-of-type selects the first element of that type regardless of position.

q: What does the CSS cascade mean?
options: CSS files load from top to bottom
The browser resolves conflicting styles using origin, specificity, and source order
Styles cascade from parent to child automatically
CSS animations play in a cascading sequence
explain: The cascade is the algorithm that determines which CSS rule wins when multiple rules target the same element. It considers origin, importance, specificity, and source order.

q: You want to make text bold in CSS. What property do you use?
options: text-weight: bold
font-weight: bold
font-style: bold
text-style: bold
explain: font-weight controls the thickness of text. Common values are normal, bold, or numeric values like 400 (normal) and 700 (bold).

q: What is the default position value for HTML elements?
options: position: relative
position: static
position: auto
position: normal
explain: All elements default to position: static which means they follow normal document flow. Top, right, bottom, left and z-index have no effect on static elements.

q: You want to make an image fill its container without stretching. What CSS do you use?
options: width: 100%; height: 100%
object-fit: cover with width: 100% and height: 100%
background-size: cover
image-fit: contain
explain: object-fit: cover scales the image to fill the container while maintaining aspect ratio, cropping if necessary. Without it the image would stretch and distort.

q: What does overflow: hidden do?
options: Hides the element from the page
Clips any content that extends beyond the element's boundaries
Prevents the element from receiving clicks
Hides the element's border
explain: overflow: hidden clips content that goes beyond the element's box. It also creates a new block formatting context which can be useful for containing floats.
